items.title: Annie Ross interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2001
items.q: There were two factions in European jazz. There was Charles Delaunay, who had the Hot Club of France... They were Dixieland bands.

ctx.x: So you got — the Hampton thing was not like your actual choice of your musical background that you’d work with. What kinds of tunes would you do with him? Would you be scatting with him and all that kind of thing?

Nope. There’s a very interesting book about Clifford Brown that came out about six months ago. And it explains it well because you know we went to Sweden and Norway and Denmark and all around. What I didn’t know was that Hamp had been told to bring a lady blues singer. Not white. And I didn’t know this. And I had my two numbers, I sang “Twisted” and I forget what else. But I was not received well. And it was wrong. It was not good for the people who were involved because at that time there were two factions in…

faction in Europe about moldy figs and how do you understand this new bebop thing and it’s not music and it doesn’t make people tap their feet and be happy and all this. So because of that my services were no longer required. And when I left, George Wallington left. We had some good times.
